zones.label: Course description
zones.summary: Course description: where the book starts. Agents build the chapters from it.
facts: Agentic workflows turn a course description into chapters, simulations, quizzes, and a learning graph.
It is part of the source. The rendered book on its own does not include it.
Publishing it lets another author start from the same description, or change it, which supports remix and regenerate.

zones.label: Learning graph
zones.summary: Learning graph: a map of the book's concepts and what each one depends on.
facts: Chapter 18 defines it as a map of the concepts of a subject, each linked to the concepts it depends on.
It is part of the source of an intelligent textbook, so retaining the book means retaining the graph too.
Publishing it supports remix and regenerate.

zones.label: Agentic skills
zones.summary: Agentic skills: reusable, documented steps an AI agent follows to build the book.
facts: Documented, reusable skills let another author regenerate a textbook from a different course description.
Platform-independent instructions can produce versions of the book across different AI tools.
Without the skills, the book is a finished artifact. With them, it can be rebuilt.

zones.label: Regenerate
zones.summary: Regenerate, the proposed sixth R: the right to recreate, update, or produce new versions of an intelligent textbook.
facts: It applies to the source (the course description, learning graph, and agentic skills), not only to the rendered book.
Test question, written for this poster: Can I recreate it from its source?
An open license on the rendered Markdown gives you the output but not the means of production. Regenerate closes that gap.
It is a proposal on the Intelligent Textbooks site. It is not part of Wiley's original framework.

The site weighed three other candidates (reason, respond, reflect) and chose regenerate. Those three describe what an AI does when a learner uses the book. Regenerate is a freedom over the book itself, like the other five.

zones.label: The book
zones.summary: The book: the rendered output that readers see and the 5Rs act on.
facts: The rendered Markdown: chapters, MicroSims, and quizzes.
Markdown output is only half the story. Without the source, the book is no more adaptable than a PDF.
David Wiley proposed the 5Rs in 2014 to describe what an open license lets you do with a finished resource like this.

zones.label: The 5Rs
zones.summary: The 5Rs: five permissions that an open license grants on the finished book.
facts: Retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. The Intelligent Textbooks site calls them cumulative: you cannot revise what you cannot retain.
The test question beside each name is the one Chapter 1 teaches.
For an AI-built book, each R gets a wider meaning. Retain, for example, includes the prompts, skills, and learning graph that generated the book.

quiz.question: Which zone is the right to recreate, update, or produce new versions of the textbook?
quiz.explanation: That is the definition of regenerate, the proposed sixth R.

quiz.question: Which zone holds the five permissions that David Wiley named?
quiz.explanation: The 5Rs describe what you may do with the finished book.

quiz.question: Which zone is the map of the book's concepts and what each one depends on?
quiz.explanation: A learning graph links each concept to the concepts it depends on.

quiz.question: Which zone is the starting point that agents turn into chapters, simulations, and quizzes?
quiz.explanation: Agentic workflows begin with the course description.

quiz.question: Which zone holds the reusable, documented steps an AI agent follows to build the book?
quiz.explanation: Those steps are the agentic skills. With them, another author can rebuild the book for a different course.

quiz.question: Which zone is the rendered output, the chapters, MicroSims, and quizzes that readers see?
quiz.explanation: The book is the output. The source is what produces it.
